title: Filtering Rows with WHERE and Logical Operators
summary: Learn to filter query results with WHERE, combine conditions using AND, OR, and NOT, control evaluation order with parentheses, and test for missing values with IS NULL.

steps.title: Filtering rows with WHERE
steps.lede: Ask a question of your data by keeping only the rows where a condition is true.

blocks.text: SELECT * FROM orders returns every order in the QuickCart database. To answer a real question — which orders took longer than 40 minutes to deliver? — you need to narrow the result to just the matching rows. WHERE takes a search condition and evaluates it for every row. A row is kept only if the condition is true; rows where it is false are discarded.

The comparison operators <, >, <=, >=, =, and <> compare two values of the same or a compatible type and produce a boolean result. = tests for equal; <> tests for not equal (!= is an alias for <>). WHERE customer_id = 2 keeps only orders from customer 2; WHERE delivery_time_minutes <> 20 keeps orders whose delivery time is not 20 minutes.

result_of.sql: SELECT order_id, customer_id, delivery_time_minutes FROM orders WHERE delivery_time_minutes > 40

after.caption: After WHERE delivery_time_minutes > 40 — only rows where the condition is true

blocks.change_summary: WHERE delivery_time_minutes > 40 keeps only the five orders whose delivery time exceeds 40 minutes; the other rows are discarded.

steps.title: Pick the right comparison operator
steps.lede: Choose the operator that matches the filter requirement.

public.prompt: You want to keep only the orders whose delivery_time_minutes is **not** 20. Which WHERE clause is correct?

options.text: WHERE delivery_time_minutes = 20
WHERE delivery_time_minutes <> 20
WHERE delivery_time_minutes > 20
WHERE delivery_time_minutes < 20

opt_a.message: = tests for equal, so this keeps only the rows where delivery_time_minutes is exactly 20 — the opposite of what you want.

opt_b.message: Correct. <> tests for not equal, so this keeps every row whose delivery_time_minutes is something other than 20. != is an alias for <> and works the same way.

opt_c.message: > keeps rows where the value is strictly greater than 20, which would miss rows with delivery_time_minutes of 15 or 18 — those are not 20 either, so they should be kept.

opt_d.message: < keeps rows where the value is strictly less than 20, which would miss rows with delivery_time_minutes of 22 or 35 — those are not 20 either, so they should be kept.

correct.message: <> (or its alias !=) is the not-equal operator. It keeps every row where the value differs from the right-hand side.

incorrect.message: Review the comparison operators: = tests for equal, <> (or !=) tests for not equal, and < > <= >= compare magnitude.

hints: Think about what the = operator does — then consider its opposite.
The glossary lists two operators that test for 'not equal': <> and its alias !=.

steps.title: Write a WHERE clause for a requirement
steps.lede: Select the WHERE clause that correctly expresses the stated filter.

public.prompt: You need a query that returns only the orders placed by customer 2. Which WHERE clause is correct?

options.text: WHERE customer_id > 2
WHERE customer_id = 2
WHERE customer_id <> 2
WHERE customer_id >= 2

opt_a.message: > keeps rows where customer_id is strictly greater than 2, so it would include customer 3 but exclude customer 2.

opt_b.message: Correct. = tests for equal, so WHERE customer_id = 2 keeps only the rows where customer_id is exactly 2.

opt_c.message: <> tests for not equal, so this keeps every customer except customer 2 — the opposite of what you want.

opt_d.message: >= keeps rows where customer_id is 2 or greater, so it would also include customer 3.

correct.message: WHERE customer_id = 2 evaluates the condition for every row and keeps only those where customer_id equals 2.

incorrect.message: Remember: WHERE keeps a row only when the condition is true for that row. = tests for exact equality.

hints: Which operator tests whether two values are exactly equal?
The condition must be true for customer 2's rows and false for all others.

tests.message_on_fail: Your query should return exactly the orders where delivery_time_minutes is greater than 40. Check your WHERE condition and the columns you are selecting.

correct.message: Your WHERE clause correctly filters to only the rows where delivery_time_minutes exceeds 40. Each row was tested individually and only the matching ones were kept.

steps.title: Combining conditions with AND, OR, and NOT
steps.lede: Join multiple filter conditions to express precise requirements.

blocks.text: A WHERE clause often needs more than one condition at once — for example, orders from customer 1 that also took longer than 30 minutes. AND, OR, and NOT let you combine boolean conditions. AND is true only when both sides are true; OR is true when at least one side is true; NOT reverses a true or false value.

result_of.sql: SELECT order_id, customer_id, delivery_time_minutes FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 1 AND delivery_time_minutes > 30 OR customer_id = 2

left.caption: Without parentheses: AND binds first, then OR

result_of.sql: SELECT order_id, customer_id, delivery_time_minutes FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 1 AND (delivery_time_minutes > 30 OR customer_id = 2)

right.caption: With parentheses: OR is evaluated first inside the group

blocks.takeaway: The same three conditions produce different result sets depending on where the parentheses go — AND always binds before OR unless you override it.

steps.title: Evaluation order and parentheses
steps.lede: NOT binds tightest, then AND, then OR — use parentheses to override.

blocks.text: Without parentheses, NOT is evaluated before AND, and AND before OR. WHERE customer_id = 1 AND delivery_time_minutes > 30 OR customer_id = 2 is read as (customer_id = 1 AND delivery_time_minutes > 30) OR customer_id = 2, keeping any order from customer 2 regardless of delivery time.

Parentheses force a different evaluation order. WHERE customer_id = 1 AND (delivery_time_minutes > 30 OR customer_id = 2) evaluates the OR first; because customer_id = 1 already rules out customer_id = 2, this version keeps only customer 1 orders that took longer than 30 minutes. NOT reverses a condition: WHERE NOT (customer_id = 1) keeps every order not from customer 1.

steps.title: Predict the result of unparenthesized conditions
steps.lede: Trace the default evaluation order to predict which rows a query returns.

public.prompt:
Consider this WHERE clause:

```sql
WHERE customer_id = 1 AND delivery_time_minutes > 30 OR customer_id = 2
```

Which description best matches what this clause keeps?

options.text: Only orders from customer 1 whose delivery took more than 30 minutes
Orders from customer 1 with delivery > 30 minutes, plus ALL orders from customer 2 regardless of delivery time
Orders from customer 1 or customer 2, but only those with delivery > 30 minutes
All orders from any customer whose delivery took more than 30 minutes

opt_a.message: This would be correct if the OR customer_id = 2 part were not there. Because AND binds before OR, the OR applies to the whole left side, so all customer 2 orders are included regardless of delivery time.

opt_b.message: Correct. AND is evaluated before OR, so the clause is read as (customer_id = 1 AND delivery_time_minutes > 30) OR customer_id = 2. The OR means any customer 2 order passes, no matter its delivery time.

opt_c.message: This would require parentheses: WHERE (customer_id = 1 OR customer_id = 2) AND delivery_time_minutes > 30. Without them, AND binds first and the OR applies to the entire left-hand expression.

opt_d.message: The delivery_time_minutes > 30 condition only applies to customer 1's rows because AND binds before OR. Customer 2's rows pass through the OR regardless of delivery time.

correct.message: AND binds before OR, so the clause groups as (customer_id = 1 AND delivery_time_minutes > 30) OR customer_id = 2. The OR lets all customer 2 orders through.

incorrect.message: Remember the precedence rule: NOT is evaluated first, then AND, then OR. Without parentheses, AND groups its two neighbours before OR is applied.

hints: Which operator has higher precedence: AND or OR?
Try mentally adding parentheses around the AND expression first, then see what the OR does.

steps.title: Use parentheses to force evaluation order
steps.lede: Choose the version of the WHERE clause that uses parentheses to match the stated requirement.

public.prompt: You want orders from **customer 1** that either took **more than 30 minutes** to deliver **or** are in the **'south'** region. Which WHERE clause correctly expresses this requirement?

options.text: WHERE customer_id = 1 AND delivery_time_minutes > 30 OR region = 'south'
WHERE customer_id = 1 AND (delivery_time_minutes > 30 OR region = 'south')
WHERE customer_id = 1 OR delivery_time_minutes > 30 AND region = 'south'
WHERE customer_id = 1 OR (delivery_time_minutes > 30 AND region = 'south')

opt_a.message: Without parentheses, AND binds first: this is read as (customer_id = 1 AND delivery_time_minutes > 30) OR region = 'south', which includes all 'south' orders regardless of customer.

opt_b.message: Correct. The parentheses force the OR to be evaluated first, so the AND then requires customer_id = 1 for the whole combined condition.

opt_c.message: AND binds before OR here too, so this reads as customer_id = 1 OR (delivery_time_minutes > 30 AND region = 'south'), which includes all customer 1 orders regardless of delivery time or region.

opt_d.message: This keeps all customer 1 orders (regardless of delivery time or region) plus any order with delivery > 30 AND region = 'south' from any customer — not what the requirement asks for.

correct.message: Parentheses around the OR force it to be evaluated before the AND, so customer_id = 1 applies to the entire combined condition.

incorrect.message: Without parentheses, AND binds before OR. To make the OR apply first, wrap it in parentheses.

hints: Write out the requirement in plain English: 'customer 1 AND (condition A OR condition B)'. The parentheses in the English map directly to SQL.
Try option A without parentheses and ask: which orders from other customers would it accidentally include?

tests.message_on_fail: Your query should return exactly the orders from customer 1 or 2 where delivery_time_minutes is greater than 30. Check your parentheses and WHERE conditions.

correct.message: Your parentheses correctly group the OR so that the AND applies to both customer conditions together. Moving the parentheses would change which rows are returned.

steps.title: Testing for missing values with IS NULL
steps.lede: Missing values are unknown — use IS NULL and IS NOT NULL, never = NULL.

blocks.text: Some orders in the QuickCart database have no recorded delivery time — the value is missing, not zero. SQL represents a missing value with NULL. NULL means unknown: it is not known whether two unknown values are equal, so testing for NULL with an ordinary comparison operator does not work.

To test whether a value is or is not null, use the predicates IS NULL and IS NOT NULL. WHERE delivery_time_minutes IS NULL finds the orders with a missing delivery time; WHERE delivery_time_minutes IS NOT NULL finds the rest.

Writing WHERE delivery_time_minutes = NULL does not test for null. NULL is not considered 'equal to' NULL, so that comparison never evaluates to true, and the query silently returns zero rows instead of the missing-time orders you meant to find.

result_of.sql: SELECT order_id, customer_id, delivery_time_minutes FROM orders WHERE delivery_time_minutes = NULL

before.caption: WHERE delivery_time_minutes = NULL — returns no rows (= NULL never evaluates to true)

result_of.sql: SELECT order_id, customer_id, delivery_time_minutes FROM orders WHERE delivery_time_minutes IS NULL

after.caption: WHERE delivery_time_minutes IS NULL — returns the two orders with a missing delivery time

blocks.change_summary: Replacing = NULL with IS NULL returns the rows with a missing delivery time; = NULL silently returns nothing because NULL is not considered equal to NULL.

steps.title: Testing for missing values (video)

segments.label: Testing for missing values with IS NULL and IS NOT NULL
segments.summary: Explains that IS NULL gives true when a value is missing and IS NOT NULL gives the opposite, written as a value or expression followed by the keywords. Slide examples on a shipping address and a price show these checks producing true or false flags. A live query then finds a row whose score is missing by using IS NULL rather than an equals sign, and a second query keeps only rows where the score is present with IS NOT NULL.

bridge.before: Watch for the rule that missing values are found with IS NULL rather than an equals sign. The clip opens directly on the definition.
bridge.after: The clip says to use IS NULL instead of equals but not why. The text above explains that a missing value is unknown, so an equals test never comes out true.

steps.title: Why does = NULL never match?
steps.lede: Explain why a query with = NULL returns no rows.

public.prompt: A developer writes `WHERE delivery_time_minutes = NULL` to find orders with a missing delivery time. The query runs without error but returns zero rows. Why?

options.text: NULL is stored as a special negative number, so = NULL compares against the wrong value.
NULL represents an unknown value; comparing an unknown to anything with = never evaluates to true, so no rows pass the filter.
The = operator only works with text columns; for numeric columns you must use IS NULL instead.
The query would return rows if there were any NULLs; the table simply has no missing delivery times.

opt_a.message: NULL is not stored as a number. It is a special marker meaning the value is unknown, not a numeric placeholder.

opt_b.message: Correct. NULL means 'unknown'. Because it is not known whether two unknown values are equal, the comparison NULL = NULL (or anything = NULL) never evaluates to true — it evaluates to NULL, which is treated as false in a WHERE clause.

opt_c.message: The = operator works with any data type. The problem is not the column type but the nature of NULL: an unknown value cannot be compared with =.

opt_d.message: The orders table does have rows with NULL delivery times (orders 1011 and 1012). The problem is that = NULL never matches them.

correct.message: NULL means 'unknown'. Because the value is unknown, comparing it with = produces NULL (not true), so no row ever passes a = NULL filter.

incorrect.message: Think about what NULL means: it is not a value, it is the absence of a known value. An equality test against an unknown result is itself unknown.

hints: What does NULL represent in SQL — a zero, an empty string, or something else?
If a value is unknown, can you know whether it equals something else?

steps.title: Recap: Filtering Rows
steps.lede: Three tools for precise row selection: WHERE, logical operators, and IS NULL.

blocks.text: WHERE evaluates a condition for every row and keeps only those where it is true. Comparison operators (<, >, <=, >=, =, <>) produce the boolean result. AND, OR, and NOT combine conditions; AND binds before OR unless you add parentheses. NULL means unknown — use IS NULL or IS NOT NULL to test for missing values; = NULL never matches.

blocks.title: Next: Sorting Results with ORDER BY
blocks.text: WHERE decides which rows come back, but not what order they appear in. Next you will use ORDER BY to sort results from slowest to fastest delivery — or any other direction you need.

remediation_steps.title: Comparison operators: which one to use
remediation_steps.lede: Each comparison operator tests a different relationship between two values.

blocks.text: The six comparison operators are <, >, <=, >=, =, and <>. = tests whether two values are equal; <> (or !=) tests whether they are not equal. < and > test strict less-than and greater-than; <= and >= include the boundary value. WHERE delivery_time_minutes > 40 keeps rows where the time is strictly above 40; WHERE delivery_time_minutes >= 40 would also keep a row with exactly 40 minutes.

remediation_steps.title: How WHERE evaluates each row
remediation_steps.lede: WHERE tests the condition against every row and keeps only those where it is true.

blocks.text: WHERE takes a search condition and evaluates it for each row in the table. A row is kept only if the condition evaluates to true; rows where it is false are discarded. SELECT order_id FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 2 keeps only the rows where customer_id equals 2 and discards every other row.

remediation_steps.title: Which rows does WHERE keep?
remediation_steps.lede: WHERE keeps a row only when the condition is true for that row.

blocks.text: Think of WHERE as a row-by-row question: for each row, is this condition true? If yes, the row appears in the result. If no, it is discarded. WHERE delivery_time_minutes > 40 asks that question for every order in the QuickCart table and returns only the orders where the delivery time is above 40 minutes.

remediation_steps.title: Default evaluation order: NOT, then AND, then OR
remediation_steps.lede: Without parentheses, AND always binds before OR — which can change the rows you get.

blocks.text: When you write multiple conditions without parentheses, SQL evaluates NOT first, then AND, then OR. WHERE customer_id = 1 AND delivery_time_minutes > 30 OR customer_id = 2 is treated as (customer_id = 1 AND delivery_time_minutes > 30) OR customer_id = 2. That keeps every order from customer 2, regardless of delivery time — which may not be what you intended.

remediation_steps.title: Using parentheses to control AND/OR grouping
remediation_steps.lede: Parentheses override the default precedence so the OR is evaluated where you need it.

blocks.text: AND, OR, and NOT combine boolean conditions. AND is true only when both sides are true; OR is true when at least one side is true. By default AND binds before OR. Adding parentheses forces the OR to be evaluated first: WHERE customer_id = 1 AND (delivery_time_minutes > 30 OR customer_id = 2) evaluates the OR group first, then applies the AND — giving a different result set.

remediation_steps.title: AND, OR, and NOT: combining conditions
remediation_steps.lede: Use AND to require both conditions, OR to accept either, and NOT to exclude.

blocks.text: AND requires both conditions to be true: WHERE customer_id = 1 AND delivery_time_minutes > 30 keeps only customer 1's slow orders. OR accepts either: WHERE customer_id = 1 OR customer_id = 2 keeps orders from either customer. NOT reverses a condition: WHERE NOT (customer_id = 1) keeps every order that is not from customer 1.

remediation_steps.title: Why = NULL never matches
remediation_steps.lede: NULL means unknown — and an unknown value is not considered equal to anything, including another unknown.

blocks.text: NULL represents an unknown value. It is not known whether two unknown values are equal, so the comparison delivery_time_minutes = NULL never evaluates to true — not even when the value is actually missing. The query runs without error but silently returns zero rows, which is not what you want when looking for missing delivery times.

remediation_steps.title: IS NULL and IS NOT NULL: the right predicates
remediation_steps.lede: Use IS NULL to find missing values and IS NOT NULL to find present ones.

blocks.text: To test whether a value is missing, use IS NULL. To test whether a value is present, use IS NOT NULL. WHERE delivery_time_minutes IS NULL returns the orders with no recorded delivery time; WHERE delivery_time_minutes IS NOT NULL returns the orders that do have one. Together these two predicates cover the whole table.
